newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman party weaker but keeps upper hand in polls.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman party weaker but keeps upper hand in polls.

text.p: Croatia's ruling nationalist party, whose popularity has sunk in advance of local elections, will beat rivals in most counties but faces defeat in the capital Zagreb, according to polls released on Thursday.

The Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), led by President Franjo Tudjman, could also lose its majority in parliament's upper House of Counties, for which voting will also be held on April 13, a poll in the independent weekly Nacional said.

But opposition coalitions in Croatia are so fragile that the HDZ could retain decisive power through deft manoeuvring in key districts such as Zagreb plus the upper House, some political analysts say.
Tudjman's party, dogged by allegations of corruption and insensitivity to the impoverishment of Croats by war that ended in 1995, looked incapable of retaining an absolute majority in most districts.

But it was likely to emerge the biggest vote getter of any party everywhere aside from the regionalist Istria peninsula. The HDZ could then retain power by seeking alliances with small parties, few of which have serious political differences with Tudjman's broad patriotic movement, which won independence for Croatia from Serbian-led Yugoslavia in a 1991 war.
Nacional's poll of 2,400 voters showed the HDZ would win an assembly majority in 14 of 21 counties by itself or in coalition. Rivals would win four with others up for grabs.

In Zagreb, with a quarter of Croatia's population and almost half the productive economy, the authoritarian Tudjman refused to recognise an opposition election victory in 1995. He exercised a "national security" veto and imposed an HDZ provisional administration that is still in office.

But critics believe he will not be able to ignore an adverse outcome this time following Croatia's admission to the democratic Council of Europe and successful popular protests against annulled election results in nearby Serbia.

The Nacional poll pointed to a two-thirds majority in Zagreb for a combined centre-left opposition. But the rival bloc is shaky. The centrist Peasant Party (HSS) has not joined because it refuses to run alongside former communists.

The main opposition Social Liberals and HSS are allied in 16 counties but not in Zagreb, where the stakes are highest. A separate poll published by the state-run Zagreb newspaper Vecernji List showed the HDZ would get just 17 percent in Split, the biggest Adriatic coast city, but an opposition bloc could count on only 15 percent.
This underlined a fragmentation of voting evident in Croatia since the end of the pro-HDZ war emergency.
More than 30 percent of voters said they were undecided in Split and in other populous provincial districts.
April's elections will be distinctive for including former rebel minority Serbs for the first time, taking in the enclave of Eastern Slavonia, which will be reintegrated under U.N.
supervision with the rest of Croatia shortly afterward.

U.N. transitional administrator Jacques Klein redrew some municipal boundaries to help Serbs gain a few local majorities, easing their fear of "absorption" or worse at the hands of the soon-to-return Croat majority, driven out in 1991.

Under Western pressure, the Croatian government has guaranteed extensive minority rights to the Serbs. Most of them have obtained Croatian citizenship papers and they have formed a moderate-led party for the elections.

Tudjman, 74, seen as "Father of the Nation" and far more popular than his party, plans to run again in presidential elections this summer despite cancer that has visibly weakened him and thinned his distinctive mane of silver hair.
